title: Poetry Mastery
subtitle: Master fixed forms, free verse, and the craft of writing an original poem

lessons.title: Les formes fixes
lessons.description: The architecture of the classical French poem: the sonnet's quatrains and tercets, the ballade's refrain and envoi, and the metrics that hold both together.

blocks.heading: Le sonnet : deux quatrains, deux tercets
blocks.body: The sonnet is fourteen lines built as two quatrains followed by two tercets. The French sonnet rhymes its quatrains ABBA ABBA (rimes embrassées) and its tercets CCD EED; the Italian, or Petrarchan, sonnet groups the same fourteen lines into an octave (ABBAABBA) and a sestet (CDECDE or CDCDCD). Somewhere between the octave and the sestet, or in the final couplet, the poem turns: this turn is the volta, and the very last line, sharpened to land hardest, is the chute.

examples.french: Le sonnet compte toujours quatorze vers, jamais un de plus.
examples.english: The sonnet always counts fourteen lines, never one more.

examples.french: Le sonnet français referme chaque quatrain sur une rime embrassée.
examples.english: The French sonnet closes each quatrain on an enclosed rhyme.

examples.french: Le sonnet italien organise ses quatorze vers en une octave, puis un sizain.
examples.english: The Italian sonnet organises its fourteen lines into an octave, then a sestet.

examples.french: La volta fait basculer le poème d'une idée vers son contraire, ou vers sa conséquence.
examples.english: The volta tips the poem from one idea toward its opposite, or toward its consequence.

examples.french: La chute doit surprendre sans jamais trahir ce que les quatrains ont installé.
examples.english: The chute must surprise without ever betraying what the quatrains set up.

blocks.tip: Read the last line of a sonnet on its own, out loud: if it lands like a small verdict, the chute is working.

blocks.heading: La ballade : strophes identiques, refrain et envoi
blocks.body: The ballade is built from three main stanzas of identical length and rhyme scheme — most often huitains (eight lines) or dizains (ten lines) — each closing on the same repeated line, the refrain. A shorter final stanza, the envoi, addresses a dedicatee directly (traditionally 'Prince') and repeats the refrain one last time, summarising the whole poem's argument in miniature.

examples.french: La ballade classique aligne trois strophes, toutes bâties sur le même schéma de rimes.
examples.english: The classical ballade lines up three stanzas, all built on the same rhyme scheme.

examples.french: Le refrain revient identique à la fin de chaque strophe, comme un vers qui refuse de changer.
examples.english: The refrain returns identical at the end of every stanza, like a line that refuses to change.

examples.french: L'envoi, plus court, s'adresse directement à un destinataire, souvent nommé « Prince ».
examples.english: The envoi, shorter, addresses a recipient directly, often named 'Prince'.

examples.french: L'envoi condense en quelques vers ce que les trois strophes ont longuement démontré.
examples.english: The envoi condenses in a few lines what the three stanzas demonstrated at length.

examples.french: Une ballade sans refrain n'est plus une ballade : elle a perdu son squelette.
examples.english: A ballade without a refrain is no longer a ballade: it has lost its skeleton.

blocks.tip: Draft the refrain line first — everything else in a ballade is written to make that one line land differently each time.

blocks.heading: Compter les syllabes : mètre et rime en poésie classique
blocks.body: French classical metrics counts syllables, not stressed beats. The alexandrin holds twelve syllables split by a caesura into two hemistiches of six; the mute e counts as a syllable before a consonant but disappears before a vowel. Rhymes are graded by how many identical sounds they share: rime pauvre shares only the final vowel, rime suffisante adds one more matching sound, and rime riche matches three sounds or more.

examples.french: L'alexandrin se coupe toujours après la sixième syllabe : c'est la césure.
examples.english: The alexandrine always breaks after the sixth syllable: that is the caesura.

examples.french: Un e muet compte pour une syllabe devant une consonne, mais s'efface devant une voyelle.
examples.english: A mute e counts as one syllable before a consonant, but disappears before a vowel.

examples.french: « Jour » et « amour » ne partagent qu'un son : c'est une rime pauvre.
examples.english: 'Jour' and 'amour' share only one sound: that is a poor rhyme.

examples.french: « Lumière » et « prière » partagent trois sons : c'est déjà une rime riche.
examples.english: 'Lumière' and 'prière' share three sounds: that already counts as a rich rhyme.

examples.french: Le décasyllabe et l'octosyllabe imposent chacun leur propre respiration au vers.
examples.english: The decasyllable and the octosyllable each impose their own breathing pattern on the line.

blocks.tip: Count on your fingers, syllable by syllable, out loud — French metrics is a spoken discipline before it is a written one.

items.example: Le sonnet impose quatorze vers répartis en deux quatrains et deux tercets.
items.exampleEnglish: The sonnet imposes fourteen lines split into two quatrains and two tercets.

items.example: La ballade se reconnaît à son refrain, répété à la fin de chaque strophe.
items.exampleEnglish: The ballade is recognised by its refrain, repeated at the end of every stanza.

items.example: Le sonnet s'ouvre toujours par deux quatrains.
items.exampleEnglish: The sonnet always opens with two quatrains.

items.example: Les deux tercets ferment le sonnet après les quatrains.
items.exampleEnglish: The two tercets close the sonnet after the quatrains.

items.example: Un distique final referme parfois le sonnet comme une porte.
items.exampleEnglish: A final couplet sometimes closes the sonnet like a door.

items.example: Chaque strophe de la ballade suit exactement le même schéma de rimes.
items.exampleEnglish: Every stanza of the ballade follows exactly the same rhyme scheme.

items.example: Chaque vers du sonnet compte exactement douze syllabes.
items.exampleEnglish: Every line of the sonnet counts exactly twelve syllables.

items.example: La rime organise le sonnet aussi sûrement que sa syntaxe.
items.exampleEnglish: The rhyme organises the sonnet as surely as its syntax does.

items.example: La rime embrassée referme chaque quatrain du sonnet français sur lui-même.
items.exampleEnglish: The enclosed rhyme closes each quatrain of the French sonnet in on itself.

items.example: La rime croisée alterne les deux sons d'un vers à l'autre.
items.exampleEnglish: The crossed rhyme alternates the two sounds from one line to the next.

items.example: La rime plate rapproche les vers deux par deux, sans les croiser.
items.exampleEnglish: The flat rhyme pairs the lines two by two, without crossing them.

items.english: the rich rhyme (three or more shared sounds)
items.example: Une rime riche demande au moins trois sons identiques entre les deux mots.
items.exampleEnglish: A rich rhyme requires at least three identical sounds between the two words.

items.english: the poor rhyme (only one shared sound)
items.example: Une rime pauvre suffit techniquement, mais elle ne surprend jamais l'oreille.
items.exampleEnglish: A poor rhyme is technically enough, but it never surprises the ear.

items.example: La rime suffisante reste la norme dans la majorité des sonnets classiques.
items.exampleEnglish: The sufficient rhyme remains the norm in most classical sonnets.

items.example: L'alexandrin reste le vers noble par excellence de la poésie française.
items.exampleEnglish: The alexandrine remains the noble line par excellence of French poetry.

items.example: Le décasyllabe précède l'alexandrin dans l'histoire du vers français.
items.exampleEnglish: The decasyllable precedes the alexandrine in the history of French verse.

items.example: L'octosyllabe donne à la ballade son pas rapide et léger.
items.exampleEnglish: The octosyllable gives the ballade its quick, light step.

items.example: On vérifie un vers en comptant ses syllabes une à une.
items.exampleEnglish: You check a line by counting its syllables one by one.

items.example: Chaque hémistiche de l'alexandrin compte exactement six syllabes.
items.exampleEnglish: Each hemistich of the alexandrine counts exactly six syllables.

items.example: La césure de l'alexandrin tombe toujours après la sixième syllabe.
items.exampleEnglish: The caesura of the alexandrine always falls after the sixth syllable.

items.english: the metre (the syllable count of a line)
items.example: Le poète a choisi un mètre unique pour tout le sonnet.
items.exampleEnglish: The poet chose a single metre for the whole sonnet.

items.example: La métrique classique impose des règles précises, presque mathématiques.
items.exampleEnglish: Classical metrics imposes precise, almost mathematical rules.

items.english: the mute e (counted in classical verse)
items.example: Le e muet se prononce devant une consonne, jamais devant une voyelle.
items.exampleEnglish: The mute e is pronounced before a consonant, never before a vowel.

items.example: Le refrain de la ballade revient, mot pour mot, à la fin de chaque strophe.
items.exampleEnglish: The ballade's refrain returns, word for word, at the end of every stanza.

items.english: the envoi (the ballade's shorter closing stanza)
items.example: L'envoi s'adresse directement au destinataire du poème.
items.exampleEnglish: The envoi addresses the poem's dedicatee directly.

items.english: the closing line, the final twist
items.example: La chute du sonnet doit tomber exactement sur le dernier mot.
items.exampleEnglish: The sonnet's closing line must land exactly on the last word.

items.english: the volta (the sonnet's turn in argument)
items.example: La volta fait basculer le sonnet entre l'octave et le sizain.
items.exampleEnglish: The volta tips the sonnet between the octave and the sestet.

items.english: the French sonnet (two quatrains, two tercets)
items.example: Le sonnet français referme ses tercets sur un schéma CCD EED.
items.exampleEnglish: The French sonnet closes its tercets on a CCD EED pattern.

items.example: Le sonnet italien place sa volta entre l'octave et le sizain.
items.exampleEnglish: The Italian sonnet places its volta between the octave and the sestet.

items.example: L'octave du sonnet italien pose le problème que le sizain va résoudre.
items.exampleEnglish: The Italian sonnet's octave sets out the problem that the sestet will resolve.

items.example: Le sizain final répond, en six vers, à la question posée par l'octave.
items.exampleEnglish: The final sestet answers, in six lines, the question posed by the octave.

items.example: La ballade classique bâtit souvent ses trois strophes sur le modèle du huitain.
items.exampleEnglish: The classical ballade often builds its three stanzas on the model of the eight-line stanza.

items.english: the rondeau (fixed form built on a refrain and two rhymes)
items.example: Le rondeau ne joue qu'avec deux rimes, mais fait revenir son premier vers en refrain.
items.exampleEnglish: The rondeau plays with only two rhymes, but brings back its first line as a refrain.

items.english: the acrostic (initial letters spell a word)
items.example: L'acrostiche cache un nom dans la première lettre de chaque vers.
items.exampleEnglish: The acrostic hides a name in the first letter of each line.

items.example: Le sonnet et la ballade comptent parmi les formes fixes les plus codifiées.
items.exampleEnglish: The sonnet and the ballade are among the most codified fixed forms.

items.example: « Lumière » rime avec « prière » sur trois sons entiers.
items.exampleEnglish: 'Lumière' rhymes with 'prière' on three whole sounds.

items.english: to versify, to put into verse
items.example: Versifier un souvenir simple demande souvent plus d'effort qu'un sujet grandiose.
items.exampleEnglish: Versifying a simple memory often takes more effort than a grand subject.

items.example: Peu de formes littéraires sont aussi codifiées que le sonnet classique.
items.exampleEnglish: Few literary forms are as codified as the classical sonnet.

blocks.heading: L'inversion et l'apostrophe lyrique
blocks.body: Classical French verse regularly inverts the normal subject-verb order to satisfy the meter or to throw weight onto a word at the rhyme. Poets also address abstract entities or absent listeners directly — the sun, the night, a dead lover — using the vocative 'ô', a construction almost extinct in ordinary speech but still alive in verse.

examples.french: Ô nuit, garde en ton sein le secret que je te confie.
examples.english: O night, keep in your bosom the secret I entrust to you.

examples.french: Ainsi passent les jours, ainsi s'effacent les visages.
examples.english: Thus pass the days, thus fade the faces.

examples.french: Grande est la nuit, et pourtant je ne crains rien.
examples.english: Great is the night, and yet I fear nothing.

examples.french: Peut-être reviendra-t-il, ce temps que l'on croyait perdu.
examples.english: Perhaps it will return, that time we thought lost.

examples.french: Telle est la loi du vers : ployer le mot sans jamais le briser.
examples.english: Such is the law of verse: to bend the word without ever breaking it.

blocks.tip: Inversion is a tool for emphasis, not decoration — use it to push the important word toward the rhyme, never at random.

blocks.heading: Les licences poétiques : apocope, élision, diérèse
blocks.body: To fit the syllable count exactly, classical poets shorten words (encor for encore), elide a final vowel before another vowel (l'âme, jusqu'à), and can split a diphthong into two syllables — diérèse — or fuse two vowels into one — synérèse — depending on what the line needs. These are not errors: they are the poet's oldest tools for controlling the count.

examples.french: Encor un jour, encor une nuit, et puis la mer nous séparera.
examples.english: One more day, one more night, and then the sea will part us.

examples.french: L'âme s'attarde où le cœur ne veut plus la suivre.
examples.english: The soul lingers where the heart no longer wishes to follow.

examples.french: Par diérèse, « li-on » compte pour deux syllabes, non pour une.
examples.english: By diaeresis, 'li-on' counts as two syllables, not one.

examples.french: Par synérèse, ce même mot se resserre en une seule syllabe.
examples.english: By synaeresis, that same word tightens into a single syllable.

examples.french: Le poète choisit la diérèse ou la synérèse selon ce que le mètre exige.
examples.english: The poet chooses diaeresis or synaeresis according to what the metre requires.

blocks.tip: When a line seems one syllable too long or too short, check first for an elidable vowel or a diérèse/synérèse choice before rewriting the whole line.

passages.title: Sonnet des constellations
passages.french:
Le ciel déploie sa carte immense de lumière,
Et sur nos fronts en feu retombe une lueur ;
Chaque étoile a gardé sa très ancienne chaleur,
Voyageuse figée dans la nuit tout entière.

Nous nommons Cassiopée une reine légère,
La Grande Ourse un chariot qui roule avec lenteur ;
Nous prêtons un visage à toute profondeur
Pour apprivoiser notre propre poussière.

Dans l'obscurité pure où s'efface notre ombre,
Nous cherchons dans le ciel un signe sans nombre,
Et le silence semble un gigantesque soir.

Chaque constellation est un conte très vieux,
Que les bergers d'antan lisaient avec les yeux,
Et que la nuit nous rend, avant le premier espoir.
passages.english:
The sky unfurls its immense map of light,
And upon our upturned faces falls a glow;
Every star has kept its ancient warmth,
A traveller frozen in the whole of night.

We call Cassiopeia a light-footed queen,
The Great Bear a chariot that rolls unhurried;
We lend a face to every depth,
To tame our own scattered dust.

In the pure darkness where our shadow fades,
We search the sky for a sign beyond counting,
And the silence seems one vast evening.

Every constellation is a very old tale,
That shepherds long ago read with their eyes,
And that the night returns to us, before the first hope.

lessons.title: Le vers libre
lessons.description: Free verse and what it frees itself from: rhyme, fixed meter, and regular punctuation — replaced by enjambment, breath, and the poem's own visual shape on the page.

blocks.heading: Le vers libre : ce qu'il abandonne, ce qu'il gagne
blocks.body: Vers libre abandons the fixed syllable count and the obligatory rhyme of classical verse; the line length is decided by breath and sense, not by a preset mètre. What is lost in external scaffolding is meant to be recovered elsewhere: in a rhythm built from repetition and syntax, in imagery that carries the weight rhyme used to carry, and in a line break that becomes, itself, a meaningful decision.

examples.french: Le vers libre ne compte plus les syllabes ; il écoute le souffle de la phrase.
examples.english: Free verse no longer counts syllables; it listens to the breath of the sentence.

examples.french: Abandonner la rime n'allège pas le travail du poète, il se déplace ailleurs.
examples.english: Abandoning rhyme does not lighten the poet's work, it merely moves elsewhere.

examples.french: Chaque retour à la ligne, en vers libre, doit se justifier par lui-même.
examples.english: Every line break, in free verse, must justify itself on its own terms.

examples.french: Sans mètre fixe, c'est l'image et la syntaxe qui portent le rythme du poème.
examples.english: Without a fixed metre, it is image and syntax that carry the poem's rhythm.

examples.french: Le vers libre reste un vers : il n'est jamais simplement de la prose découpée au hasard.
examples.english: Free verse remains verse: it is never simply prose chopped up at random.

blocks.tip: Before cutting a line, ask what the break itself adds — suspense, emphasis, a held breath. If the answer is nothing, the line is prose in disguise.

blocks.heading: L'enjambement, le rejet, le contre-rejet
blocks.body: Enjambement lets a sentence run past the end of a line without pause, creating tension between the line's visual stop and the sentence's real continuation. When only a short fragment spills over onto the next line, that fragment is called a rejet; when a short fragment is instead held back at the end of one line before the sentence properly begins on the next, that is a contre-rejet. Both devices let a poet isolate a single word for maximum weight.

examples.french: L'enjambement crée une tension entre la fin du vers et la fin de la phrase.
examples.english: Enjambment creates a tension between the end of the line and the end of the sentence.

examples.french: Le rejet isole un mot bref, rejeté seul au début du vers suivant.
examples.english: The rejet isolates a brief word, thrown alone to the start of the next line.

examples.french: Le contre-rejet retient un mot en fin de vers, juste avant que la phrase ne commence vraiment.
examples.english: The contre-rejet holds a word back at the end of the line, just before the sentence truly begins.

examples.french: Un enjambement bien placé fait attendre le lecteur une fraction de seconde de trop.
examples.english: A well-placed enjambment makes the reader wait a fraction of a second too long.

examples.french: Sans enjambement, le vers libre perdrait l'un de ses effets les plus précis.
examples.english: Without enjambment, free verse would lose one of its most precise effects.

blocks.tip: Read a suspected enjambment aloud without stopping at the line break — if the sentence needs that pause to make sense, it is not a true enjambment.

blocks.heading: La disposition sur la page : blancs, ponctuation, forme
blocks.body: Modern free verse often treats the blank space of the page itself as expressive: irregular indentation, a typographic gap standing in for a pause no punctuation mark could render, or — in the extreme case of the calligramme — words arranged to draw the very shape they describe. Many free-verse poets also drop capital letters and end punctuation altogether, letting the line break alone carry what a comma or a full stop used to carry.

examples.french: Le blanc typographique tient parfois lieu de silence, là où la ponctuation serait trop lourde.
examples.english: Typographic white space sometimes stands in for silence, where punctuation would be too heavy.

examples.french: Le calligramme dispose les mots de façon à dessiner ce qu'ils racontent.
examples.english: The calligram arranges words so as to draw what they describe.

examples.french: Sans majuscule ni point final, la phrase semble ne jamais vraiment commencer ni finir.
examples.english: Without a capital letter or a full stop, the sentence seems never quite to begin or end.

examples.french: La mise en page d'un poème en vers libre fait déjà partie du sens.
examples.english: The layout of a free-verse poem is already part of its meaning.

examples.french: Une phrase nominale, sans verbe, suffit parfois à fixer une image entière.
examples.english: A nominal sentence, without a verb, is sometimes enough to fix an entire image.

blocks.tip: Try reading a free-verse poem with all punctuation restored in your head — if the ambiguity disappears, the poet removed it on purpose.

items.example: Le vers libre abandonne la rime et le compte fixe de syllabes.
items.exampleEnglish: Free verse abandons rhyme and the fixed syllable count.

items.english: the rejet (a short fragment spilling onto the next line)
items.example: Le rejet isole un seul mot, rejeté au tout début du vers suivant.
items.exampleEnglish: The rejet isolates a single word, thrown to the very start of the next line.

items.english: the contre-rejet (a short fragment held at the end of the line before it)
items.example: Le contre-rejet retient un mot en fin de vers, juste avant que la phrase ne s'ouvre vraiment.
items.exampleEnglish: The contre-rejet holds a word at the end of the line, just before the sentence truly opens.

items.english: the enjambment (a sentence spilling onto the next line)
items.example: L'enjambement crée une tension entre le sens et la fin du vers.
items.exampleEnglish: The enjambment creates a tension between meaning and the end of the line.

items.english: the verset (a long, breath-length free-verse line)
items.example: Le verset s'étire sur une respiration entière, sans se soucier du compte des syllabes.
items.exampleEnglish: The verset stretches over one whole breath, unconcerned with the syllable count.

items.example: Le poème en prose renonce même à la ligne courte, mais garde l'image et le rythme.
items.exampleEnglish: The prose poem gives up even the short line, but keeps the image and the rhythm.

items.example: Chaque strophe libre du poème s'arrête là où le souffle s'arrête, non là où la règle l'exige.
items.exampleEnglish: Each free-form stanza of the poem stops where the breath stops, not where the rule demands.

items.english: the breath, the breathing pace (of a line)
items.example: En vers libre, c'est le souffle qui décide où finit le vers, non le compte des syllabes.
items.exampleEnglish: In free verse, it is the breath that decides where the line ends, not the syllable count.

items.english: the anaphora (repeating a word or phrase at the start of successive lines)
items.example: L'anaphore martèle le même mot au début de chaque verset.
items.exampleEnglish: The anaphora hammers the same word at the start of every verset.

items.example: L'allitération en « s » fait presque siffler le vers libre.
items.exampleEnglish: The alliteration in 's' makes the free-verse line almost hiss.

items.example: Sans rime, l'assonance suffit parfois à lier deux vers entre eux.
items.exampleEnglish: Without rhyme, assonance is sometimes enough to link two lines together.

items.example: La répétition remplace ici la rime comme principe d'unité.

items.english: the litany (a poetic device of insistent repetition)

items.example: Sans rime pour les tenir, les images poétiques doivent se répondre entre elles.

items.example: Une image insolite frappe précisément parce qu'elle n'était pas attendue.

items.example: Une phrase nominale isolée peut fixer une image mieux qu'une longue description.

items.example: Le style elliptique du poème force le lecteur à combler les vides.

items.example: La forme fragmentaire du poème imite le désordre d'une pensée nocturne.
items.exampleEnglish: The poem's fragmentary form imitates the disorder of a nighttime thought.

items.example: Un vers libre reste un vers, même sans rime ni mètre fixe.

items.exampleEnglish: Free verse was born of a resolutely modern gesture: breaking with tradition.

blocks.heading: La phrase nominale et l'ellipse du verbe
blocks.body: Free verse frequently drops the verb altogether, presenting a bare noun phrase as a complete poetic unit. This nominal sentence works because a line of poetry does not need to be a grammatical sentence to be understood; it needs only to land as a complete thought. The same economy governs ellipsis more broadly: a poet may omit a connector, an article, even a whole clause, trusting the line break to supply the missing logic.

examples.french: Une fenêtre allumée. Une ville qui ne dort jamais tout à fait.
examples.english: A lit window. A city that never quite sleeps.

examples.french: Le vent, encore. Et rien d'autre à dire.
examples.english: The wind, again. And nothing else to say.

examples.french: Trop de silence pour un seul cœur.
examples.english: Too much silence for a single heart.

examples.french: Des rues, des chats, des volets qui claquent — et moi qui compte.
examples.english: Streets, cats, shutters slamming — and me, counting.

examples.french: Pas un mot. Juste la lumière, tenace, au sixième étage.
examples.english: Not a word. Just the light, stubborn, on the sixth floor.

blocks.tip: A nominal sentence works only if the missing verb is genuinely recoverable from context — remove too much and the line becomes merely unclear, not evocative.

blocks.heading: La ponctuation libérée : minuscule et absence de point
blocks.body: Many free-verse poets abandon the capital letter at the start of a line and the full stop at the end of a sentence, letting the line break alone signal a pause. This is a deliberate choice, not carelessness: it keeps a phrase open to more than one reading, and it lets one clause bleed into the next without the visual interruption a period would create.

lessons.title: Écrire un poème
lessons.description: From first spark to finished page: drawing on lived experience, drafting, reading aloud to test the sound, and revising until the chute finally lands.

blocks.heading: Du vécu à la première image
blocks.body: A poem rarely begins with a theme; it begins with a precise, concrete detail drawn from lived experience — a smell, a gesture, an overheard sentence — that the poet trusts to carry more than it seems to. The temptation at C2 is to reach immediately for grand abstractions (l'amour, le temps, la mort); resist it, and let one small image do the work those abstractions would only flatten.

examples.french: Un poème ne part presque jamais d'une idée abstraite, mais d'un détail précis.
examples.english: A poem almost never starts from an abstract idea, but from a precise detail.

examples.french: Le vécu fournit la matière ; le travail du poète est de la transposer, non de la raconter telle quelle.
examples.english: Lived experience supplies the material; the poet's job is to transpose it, not simply recount it as it happened.

examples.french: Une seule image bien choisie porte plus qu'un paragraphe entier d'explications.
examples.english: One well-chosen image carries more than a whole paragraph of explanations.

examples.french: S'inspirer de sa propre vie n'oblige pas à tout dire : le silence choisit aussi.
examples.english: Drawing inspiration from one's own life does not require telling everything: silence also makes choices.

examples.french: L'atelier d'écriture commence souvent par une contrainte simple : décrire un objet, sans le nommer.
examples.english: The writing workshop often begins with a simple constraint: describe an object without naming it.

blocks.tip: Write down the concrete detail before you know what the poem is 'about' — the theme usually reveals itself only after several drafts.

blocks.heading: Le brouillon, la lecture à voix haute, la réécriture
blocks.body: A first draft exists to be wrong in interesting ways: write it fast, without judging it, then set it aside. The single most reliable revision tool is reading the poem aloud — the ear catches a clumsy sonority, an accidental rhyme, an overlong line, that the eye alone would miss. Rewriting is not correcting typos; it is often replacing a whole image, cutting a line that only explains what another line already shows, and polishing a line until each word earns its place.

examples.french: Le brouillon existe pour se tromper vite : on le corrige après, jamais pendant.
examples.english: The draft exists to make mistakes quickly: you correct it afterwards, never during.

examples.french: La lecture à voix haute révèle des maladresses que l'œil seul ne voit jamais.
examples.english: Reading aloud reveals clumsy moments that the eye alone never catches.

examples.french: Réécrire, ce n'est pas corriger des fautes : c'est parfois remplacer une image entière.
examples.english: Rewriting is not correcting mistakes: it is sometimes replacing a whole image.

examples.french: Polir un vers, mot après mot, jusqu'à ce que chacun mérite sa place.
examples.english: Polishing a line, word by word, until each one earns its place.

examples.french: Une bonne relecture supprime plus de vers qu'elle n'en ajoute.
examples.english: A good rereading removes more lines than it adds.

blocks.tip: Read the draft aloud to someone else, even once — a listener's silence at the wrong moment tells you more than a week of private rereading.

blocks.heading: Trouver la chute, choisir un titre, assembler un recueil
blocks.body: The final line deserves as much drafting as the first — many poets write several candidate chutes before finding the one that closes the poem without simply summarising it. The title is not a label added at the end; a well-chosen title can reframe every line that follows it, so it is worth drafting and rewriting in parallel with the poem itself. A finished poem, in turn, is rarely published alone: it finds its full meaning inside a recueil, in conversation with the poems placed just before and after it.

examples.french: Trouver la chute demande souvent d'écrire cinq fins avant de garder la bonne.
examples.english: Finding the chute often means writing five endings before keeping the right one.

examples.french: Un bon titre ne résume pas le poème : il en change discrètement la lecture.
examples.english: A good title does not summarise the poem: it discreetly changes how it is read.

examples.french: Une dédicace, en tête de poème, oriente aussi la lecture sans l'imposer.
examples.english: A dedication, at the head of a poem, also steers the reading without forcing it.

examples.french: Un poème seul se lit autrement qu'un poème placé dans un recueil.
examples.english: A poem read alone reads differently from a poem placed inside a collection.

examples.french: Oser publier, c'est accepter qu'un lecteur inconnu termine le poème à sa manière.
examples.english: Daring to publish means accepting that an unknown reader will finish the poem in their own way.

blocks.tip: Draft your title last, but place it first — read the whole poem once more under that exact title before deciding it is finished.

blocks.heading: L'impératif et le subjonctif de l'atelier d'écriture
blocks.body: Writing-workshop advice favours the imperative for concrete instructions (choisis, relis, supprime) and the subjunctive after impersonal expressions like il faut que or il vaut mieux que when the advice is a recommendation rather than an order. This register suggests without dictating — exactly the tone a poet giving feedback to another poet needs.

examples.french: Relis ton poème à voix haute avant d'y toucher encore.
examples.english: Reread your poem aloud before touching it again.

examples.french: Choisis un seul détail, et laisse tout le reste au silence.
examples.english: Choose a single detail, and leave everything else to silence.

examples.french: Il faut que tu supprimes ce vers : il explique ce que l'image montrait déjà.
examples.english: You need to cut that line: it explains what the image already showed.

examples.french: Il vaut mieux que la chute reste ambiguë plutôt qu'elle ne conclue trop nettement.
examples.english: It is better for the chute to stay ambiguous than for it to conclude too neatly.

examples.french: N'explique jamais une image : fais-lui confiance.
examples.english: Never explain an image: trust it.

blocks.tip: Save the imperative for concrete, actionable steps; reach for il faut que / il vaut mieux que when you are recommending a judgment call, not a fact.

blocks.heading: Le conditionnel de suggestion et les verbes pronominaux de la réécriture
blocks.body: Gentle workshop suggestions are often phrased in the conditional — on pourrait, il conviendrait de — which softens a critique into an open possibility rather than a verdict. The revision process itself is frequently described with reflexive, pronominal verbs (se relire, se corriger, se reprendre), which frame rewriting as something the poet does to their own text, almost as a private conversation.

examples.french: On pourrait peut-être resserrer cette strophe, sans rien lui retirer d'essentiel.
examples.english: One could perhaps tighten this stanza, without taking away anything essential.

examples.french: Il conviendrait de retravailler la chute, qui arrive un peu trop tôt.
examples.english: It would be worth reworking the chute, which arrives a little too early.

examples.french: Le poète se relit à voix haute, seul, avant de montrer le texte à quiconque.
examples.english: The poet rereads themself aloud, alone, before showing the text to anyone.

examples.french: Elle se reprend trois fois sur le même vers, sans jamais se satisfaire.
examples.english: She corrects herself three times on the same line, never quite satisfied.

examples.french: On aurait pu garder la première version ; on a préféré la deuxième, plus sobre.
examples.english: One could have kept the first version; the second, sparer one was preferred.

blocks.tip: Use the conditional when you want feedback to remain a suggestion the writer can reject — it keeps the poem theirs, not yours.

passages.title: Du brouillon au poème
passages.french:
Un poème ne commence presque jamais par une grande idée.
Il commence par un détail : une odeur, un geste, une phrase surprise dans la rue.
Le poète débutant croit qu'il doit d'abord savoir de quoi il va parler.
Le plus souvent, c'est l'inverse : le sujet se révèle en écrivant, jamais avant.
Le brouillon accueille toutes les maladresses, sans exception et sans honte.
On y jette des images, on en garde une sur dix, parfois moins.
Vient ensuite la lecture à voix haute, seule étape vraiment irremplaçable.
L'œil pardonne ce que l'oreille refuse net : une sonorité ratée, un vers trop long.
Réécrire ne consiste pas à corriger des fautes de grammaire.
C'est souvent remplacer une image entière par une autre, plus juste.
C'est aussi accepter de supprimer un vers auquel on tenait, parce qu'il explique ce qu'une autre image montrait déjà.
La chute, elle, se travaille à part : on écrit parfois cinq fins avant de garder la bonne.
Le titre vient rarement en premier, même s'il se lit en tête du poème.
Un bon titre ne raconte pas le poème : il en oriente discrètement la lecture.
Enfin, publier demande un peu de courage, car le poème cesse alors d'appartenir tout à fait à son auteur.
Un lecteur inconnu le lira à sa manière, et cette lecture-là comptera autant que la première.
passages.english:
A poem almost never begins with a grand idea.
It begins with a detail: a smell, a gesture, a sentence overheard in the street.
The beginning poet believes they must first know what they are going to write about.
Most often, it is the opposite: the subject reveals itself while writing, never before.
The draft welcomes every clumsy attempt, without exception and without shame.
You throw in images, keep one in ten, sometimes fewer.
Then comes reading aloud, the one truly irreplaceable step.
The eye forgives what the ear flatly refuses: a failed sonority, an overlong line.
Rewriting does not consist of correcting grammar mistakes.
It is often replacing a whole image with another, truer one.
It is also accepting the loss of a line you were attached to, because it explained what another image already showed.
The chute, for its part, is worked separately: sometimes five endings are written before the right one is kept.
The title rarely comes first, even though it is read at the head of the poem.
A good title does not retell the poem: it discreetly steers how it is read.
Finally, publishing takes a little courage, because the poem then stops belonging entirely to its author.
An unknown reader will read it in their own way, and that reading will matter just as much as the first.
